Title: Jeremy Bowen: Myanmar genocide verdict is historic and could have far-reaching implications
URL: https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6ly58ndgd0no

<article>
The court's landmark decision also reinforces those who believe in the rules that were made to regulate the way that power is wielded after World War Two. The 1948 Genocide Convention was a vital part of the structure that was built around the United Nations to stop a repeat of the unfettered brutality, war and genocide in the years before the defeat of the Nazis.

The rules and conventions established after 1945 have been under unprecedented pressure in the era of US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping. On the day of their summit in China, the ICJ issued a reminder that international law still exists and perhaps can show that the use of force against civilians has consequences.

Lawyers will study the way in which The Gambia proved the crucial point that the state of Myanmar intended to commit genocide.

It has called for an urgent session of the Security Council, is expelling Myanmar's defence attaché in London and has promised other measures in the coming days.

Not much might be possible at the UN. A tough resolution against Myanmar could be vetoed by either China or Russia, or both.

Other rumblings have come from the Trump Administration about the case. Without waiting for the ICJ's verdict, former US President Joe Biden's administration declared in 2022 that the Myanmar military committed genocide against the Rohingya people.
</article>

Title: Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say
URL: https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckzd9nln5e6go

<article>
**European leaders have said they are ready for negotiations with Russia on ending the war in Ukraine, in a strong show of support for Kyiv.**

"Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic".

They were speaking at Berlin's summit of Ukraine's allies known as the Coalition of the Willing.

Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, one of the two US envoys who were in Berlin, said the US president wanted to make a deal with Moscow "with Europe by his side". Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US-led peace talks.

Trump had earlier held historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen, south-eastern China, with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping and later dialled into the Berlin summit from Air Force One.

In a lengthy press conference following his talks with Trump and Xi, Putin addressed the question of multilateral peace talks, saying the Americans were "insistently" asking Russia to allow the Europeans to take part.

Putin claimed Russia was not against the idea but said Moscow wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks".

"That is why, through diplomatic channels, we have invited the Europeans to come to Moscow in order to determine their positions. And after that, we will decide in what format we will continue the dialogue with Ukraine."

But Putin also said that "every day" Russia heard that European leaders were talking about war coming in 2030. "But we are not planning to attack anyone... Is that normal? I do not think so," he said. Still, Putin added, Russia understood that "discussing issues linked to security in Europe is pointless without the Europeans".

Jared Kushner told reporters that the US president had come away from Shenzhen believing that "peace is achievable".

Striking an upbeat note, Kushner said that the Russians were willing to trust the instinct of the US envoys "on our behalf" that the Europeans should be at the table and that Moscow was now "comfortable" with Ukraine having security guarantees based on the idea enshrined in Nato's Article Five that requires allies to come to a country's defence if it comes under attack.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who also was at the summit in Germany's capital, has long sought a guarantee equivalent to Nato's collective defence clause, and there has been little indication that Putin would accept that kind of condition.

Russia rejects outright the idea of Ukrainian membership of Nato, but reports say US negotiators have mulled the idea of giving Kyiv Article Five-style guarantees without being part of the Western defensive alliance if it agrees to painful territorial concessions.

Zelensky and the three European leaders – Merz, Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron – were not as upbeat as Kushner, and the Ukrainian president made clear that the Russian president had spurned every proposal so far: "Putin has always said no."

The German chancellor was equally sceptical, although he said with US involvement the chance of peace was increasing. Europe was willing to enter "serious discussions on European security" with Russia, he explained, "as long as it's matched with a serious discussion and only first a peace agreement with Ukraine".

"These talks have to begin, and we will accept if conditions are acceptable for Europe and Ukraine," said Merz.

He also said any attempts to divide Europe into spheres of influence run by major powers was unacceptable, amid concerns on the continent that this issue may have been on the agenda at the trilateral talks in Shenzhen.

"The US understands that there can be no peace without us. We, in turn, know that with the United States by our side, the prospects for peace increase," Merz added.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk also took exception to Trump's description of Putin as a "friend" at the Shenzhen summit, saying: "Mr Putin is not our friend and will never be."

Meanwhile, Macron urged Ukraine's allies to do the "maximum" to deliver the much-needed air defence systems Kyiv needed to repel deadly Russian attacks.

The French leader also urged the allies to "reopen the question" of Ukraine's membership in Nato.

There have been mixed messages from Moscow on European participation to the talks. Last week, following a visit to Moscow, the US envoys, Steve Witkoff and Kushner, appeared certain that Europe would soon have a seat at the negotiating table.

But the Russians were more circumspect and this week Putin's aide Yury Ushakov said a "great deal" would have to be done before the format could be expanded, suggesting that several more rounds of discussions would have to be held before any four-sided talks could take place.

Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

While Russia has engaged with several rounds of talks over the last year, little in Moscow's rhetoric or actions suggests that the Kremlin is considering scaling down its war on Ukraine.

It continues to pound Kyiv's energy infrastructure to cripple it as winter takes hold, increasing numbers of civilian casualties are being recorded across the country, and Kremlin officials have not budged from Russia's demands for Ukrainian sovereign territory.

As delegations were meeting in China and Germany on Thursday, several buildings in Kyiv's historic centre came under attack from drones. One person was killed in a strike on a residential building in the Podilskyi neighbourhood, while the Dutch and Austrian embassies as well as Saint Volodymyr's Cathedral reported damage.

And Putin also vowed that Moscow's response to a Ukrainian strike on the Crimean Bridge linking Russia with occupied Crimea would be "considerably more painful" than what Kyiv had achieved.

He also said he had discussed a "possible ceasefire in a number of areas" but had decided against it after the attack on the bridge.

Still, Putin claimed to be "interested" in ending the war and was ready to make compromises, while Ukraine and Europe were not.

"I assure you, we have no desire at all to continue this armed conflict," Putin said, despite the fact that Russia has in recent months intensified its attacks on Ukraine's critical infrastructure as cold winter approaches.

Kyiv and its European allies say that – in the absence of any major success on the vast front line – the Kremlin leader is seeking to break Ukrainian resistance by leaving millions of civilians without electricity and water supply.
</article>

Title: 'They're doing their best to cope' - Ukrainians in Berkshire
URL: https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj5y14ge2xvxo

<article>
- Published

**More than four-and-a-half years on from the start of Ukraine-Russian war, a leading figure in Reading's Ukrainian community centre has reflected on how refugees have assimilated.**

Mick Polleck said some arrivals have moved out of Reading and into neighbouring counties as their lives have progressed since they moved to the UK.

It is thought about 2,800 Ukrainians arrived in Berkshire after the invasion in February 2022, but some have decided to return home.

"They're doing their best to cope given that for the majority of them their husbands, brothers, fathers even, are still back home defending the country. It's bittersweet," Polleck said.

"\[Some\] had something like a couple of hours to leave \[their homes\].

"Those poor people who come from eastern Ukraine, from the Donbas and so on, their homes have not been occupied by Russians. Their homes have been destroyed.

"Obviously, they would like to go back and rebuild but that will all depend on what those frightening three people \[Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping\] \[were\] discussing in China \[on Thursday\]."

Speaking to BBC Radio Berkshire from Ukraine's capital Kyiv, the BBC's world affairs editor John Simpson said it was "pretty tense" but that it is "nothing unusual" for its residents who have lived it for years.

"If you came here and you and I walked down the street, I don't think you would realise it was a city at war. That's the nature of modern warfare," he said.
</article>

Title: Russia targets Kyiv crossings days after Ukraine hits Crimean Bridge
URL: https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6x29gn4pdn9o

<article>
**Russia targeted bridges in Kyiv and railway stations overnight in a major attack launched days after Ukraine badly damaged the strategically important Crimean Bridge.**

Ballistic missiles hit key crossings in the capital during a nationwide assault which Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said was "one of the most massive strikes" of the war so far and left at least nine dead.

Russian President Vladimir Putin had threatened to retaliate for the attack on the Crimean Bridge, which the Kremlin built to link Russia and the occupied Crimean peninsula.

The latest Russian strikes coincided with talks around the war, and came as the Kremlin pushed back against a US claim that Russia could be open to Western-backed security guarantees for Ukraine.

The overnight attack against Ukraine was spread across several cities and regions, Zelensky said, with residential buildings and energy facilities also hit.

Air raid sirens lasted non-stop throughout the night and were ongoing into the morning.

Zelensky said over 110 missiles and more than 400 attack drones were launched by Russia, adding that "particularly insidious" tactics to launch the waves in 20 to 30-minute internals made it "more difficult to extinguish fires, clear debris, and restore services".

The three bridges targeted in Kyiv - the Podilsko-Voskresensky Bridge, the Darnytskyi Bridge and the Southern Bridge - were closed to traffic.

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko urged people to "avoid travelling into the city by private car unless absolutely necessary", adding to the disruption around the capital following a first round of strikes against vital crossings earlier this week.

At least seven people were killed and 17 more were injured, Klitschko added, with unspecified civilian facilities also hit.

Ukraine's major operation to take out the road section of the Crimean Bridge earlier this week was a tactical and symbolic blow for Moscow.

Since illegally annexing Crimea in 2014, Moscow has housed troops and military equipment there, with occupying forces travelling through the peninsula towards the front line.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said an operation to weaken the bridge's defences and ultimately cause part of it to collapse had been weeks in the making.

Russian President Vladimir Putin - who personally opened the bridge in 2019 to international condemnation - said the Kremlin's retaliation for the strike would be "far more painful".

Of the nine fatalities confirmed so far, seven were in Kyiv and two were in Lviv, with at least 28 people injured.

The Sknyliv railway station in Lviv, a city in western Ukraine which has become one of the primary entry points to Ukraine for people and international aid, was badly damaged, the city's Mayor Andriy Sadovyi said.

The attack began hours after European leaders including UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said they were ready for negotiations involving Moscow to end the war in Ukraine.

The Berlin meeting of the so-called coalition of the willing, an international alliance of Ukraine's allies committed to providing security support in the event of a peace deal, was attended by Zelensky and US President Donald Trump's envoys.

Jared Kushner said the US "wants to make a deal with Europe by his side" after fears of an agreement negotiated between the US and Russia were reignited by Trump's one-to-one talks with Putin earlier this week.

He claimed Russia was "comfortable" with Ukraine having security guarantees based on Nato's Article Five, which requires allies to come to a country's defence if it comes under attack.

On Monday, Russia's deputy foreign minister Sergei Ryabkov pushed back against that, saying "quasi-Nato" membership for Ukraine would be "unacceptable" to Russia. The Kremlin has long cited the prospect of Ukraine joining Nato as a key justification for its war effort.

The US president dialled into the Berlin talks from Air Force One on his way back from China, where he met his Russian counterpart and Chinese leader Xi Jinping.

He reportedly questioned the decision of European leaders to commit €70bn (£58.6bn; $76.bn) in military funding for Ukraine.

The UK and France are jointly leading the first military exercise organised by the coalition of the willing, which involves thousands of troops from 11 countries and is taking place in Poland.

On Friday, Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk accused Russia of an "intentional provocation" after a Russian cruise missile landed in his country.

It struck around 50km (31 miles) from its border with Ukraine, the Polish Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said on Friday.

Two more unidentified projectiles, suspected to be a drone and a second missile, landed in villages nearby and no one was harmed, he added.

Polish and Swedish jets were scrambled on Nato's eastern flank as Russia's attack on western Ukraine continued. They have since been stood down.

France's foreign minister Jean-Noël Barro has called for a meeting of the UN Security Council following Russia's attack on Kyiv.

He described the strikes, which reportedly damaged the Austrian and Dutch embassies, as "crimes" that "Russia will have to answer for".
</article>

Title: Russian missile hits Poland as Ukraine's allies hold military exercise, says Tusk
URL: https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqx2x9dklxnro

<article>
**Poland says a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace early on Friday, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk saying it did not appear to be an accident when Western military exercises were taking place in the region.**

Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.

Russia has made no comment about the violations, which took place during one of its biggest aerial attacks on Ukraine since the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022.

Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said the Kh-101 missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec in southeastern Poland about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border.

The cruise missile, designed for precision targets, crashed at about 06:30 (5:30GMT) and Natalie Szponar, a local resident, said she was getting her children ready for school when she heard a "whistle and a dull impact".

Another suspected missile went down near Rudnik nad Sanem to the west of Nowy Lipowiec, and a jet-powered drone crashed to the south near Mołodycz, said Kosiniak-Kamysz.

He called the incursion into Polish airspace a "provocation" from Russia and said he would be asking Nato for additional support.

Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned "grave violations of Polish airspace" and said Nato jets had been scrambled in response. "This incident is clearly dangerous - a consequence of Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine," said Rutte, who was due to visit Warsaw on Saturday.

A UK- and France-led exercise called Koalicja 2026 is currently taking place in southeastern Poland involving 11 countries that are part of the West's Coalition of the Willing group in preparation for a potential peace deal in Ukraine.

"It is no coincidence that these objects landed near the site where military manoeuvres by a 'coalition of the willing' supported by Polish troops are taking place in Nowa Dęba," Tusk told reporters on Friday.

Hours later, five coalition defence ministers - from the UK, France, Poland, Estonia and Lithuania - visited the military training ground where the drill was taking place.

UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting told reporters that what had happened earlier was "yet another example of Russian provocation that is designed to divide Europe and to deter Ukraine's allies from supporting their fight for freedom and democracy".

In Brussels, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the missile incident was "utterly unacceptable".

European Council President António Costa expressed his "strong solidarity" with the Polish people and said Russia had to come to the negotiating table to bring the war to the end.

The violations of Polish airspace came a day after 40 countries took part in a Coalition of the Willing summit in Berlin, where the allies pledged continued support for Kyiv, and Chancellor Friedrich Merz said peace talks with Russia should take place soon on neutral territory.

At least eight people were killed on Friday as Russian missiles and drones targeted three of Kyiv's bridges across the River Dnipro and a station in Lviv, days after Russia's Vladimir Putin threatened "painful" retaliation for repeated strikes on Russia's bridge across the Kerch Strait to occupied Crimea.

Russia also launched an apparent double tap attack on the busy centre of the Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih.

The Chairman of the Kryvyi Rih Defense Council, Oleksandr Vilkul, said two people were killed in the shelling, including a 20-year-old woman and a seven-year-old boy, and at least 40 people have been injured.

This is not the first time the war in Ukraine has spilled over into Poland. In July a cruise missile also landed in Poland, leaving a 10m-wide (33ft) crater. That incident also took place during an attack on the western Ukrainian city of Lviv.

Casualties in Poland have been rare, while Ukraine suffers deadly attacks on a daily basis. However, two Polish farmers were killed by a missile in November 2022, which was believed to have been a Ukrainian air-defence missile responding to a Russian attack.

Moldovan officials said on Friday that their airspace had also been violated on Friday, when a drone crossed briefly into its territory during Russia's attacks on Ukraine.

The Moldovan defence ministry has recorded 118 such violations since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.
</article>

Title: Zelensky says Putin is a 'killer' after Trump calls Russian leader a friend
URL: https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cxnv4zvmdy0jo

<article>
- Published

**Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has said Vladimir Putin is a "killer" in response to Donald Trump referring to the Russian leader as his "friend" in China this week.**

Speaking to CNN, Zelensky said it was up to the US president "how to call Putin" but "for us, he is an enemy... for us, he's a killer".

Before Thursday's historic trilateral meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Putin, Trump called Putin his "friend" and said the two leaders have had a "great relationship for many years".

Russian attacks continued overnight, with two people killed, including a boy, and 52 injured in missile and drone strikes on Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih in the central Dnipropetrovsk region, officials said.

Ukraine's state emergency service DSNS said 11 people were also injured in the north-eastern Kharkiv region, and one person in Rivne, in the north-west.

On Friday, at least nine people were killed in Russian strikes targeting bridges in the capital Kyiv and railway stations in western Ukraine - with Zelensky calling the attack the "biggest this year" after an onslaught of 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic, and more than 400 drones.

The strikes came days after Ukraine had badly damaged the Crimean Bridge.

Hours after Friday's strikes on Ukraine, Trump told reporters at the White House that Putin would "love to end the war".

"They \[Zelensky and Putin\] both want to end it and it's a very good thing I have a relationship," he said on Friday.

Trump also doubled down on his description of the Russian leader as a friend but said he "can't speak" to whether Putin is a friend to the US.

However Zelensky said despite Trump's stance, he saw Putin as "a killer".

"I think mostly for the people in the world, he is a killer because he's killing - by the way- he's killing each day and night," he told CNN.

Zelensky also said speaking about Putin like he was a "friend" meant "he doesn't feel enough pressure".

The war of words came as neighbouring Poland said a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace in the south-east of the country early on Friday.

Polish Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said the missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border.

This was about 100km from where European troops - from 11 of the 36 member nations of the coalition of the willing - were completing a training exercise, Polish authorities said. Another cruise missile and a jet-powered drone were suspected to have hit two other locations, they added.

On Saturday, Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski told the BBC the cruise missiles had guidance systems, so "it is very unlikely that they veered off course as a result of Ukrainian electronic warfare".

"This is a war in Europe that affects our security," he told Radio 4's Today programme, also referencing similar incidents in recent months across Europe.

Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.

Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned "grave violations of Polish airspace" and said the military alliance had scrambled its jets in response.

Russia has made no comment about the violations, which took place during Friday's massive attack on Ukraine.

Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
</article>

Title: Denmark accuses Russia of plotting to assassinate US-Ukrainian rapper
URL: https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmde1lj4yjxno

<article>
- Published

**Denmark has accused Russian intelligence services of plotting to assassinate a Ukrainian-American near Copenhagen, saying they had "planned" and "initiated" the attempt.**

Denmark's security and intelligence agency (PET) said it had stopped individuals who were intending to kill the person, named by Danish media as rapper Kyivstoner, at a concert in September. Two people were charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service, and pleaded not guilty.

Denmark's foreign minister said Russia's defence attaché will now be expelled.

Russia's embassy in Denmark called the allegations "unsubstantiated" and said Copenhagen failed to provide evidence of Moscow's involvement.

In a statement, the embassy claimed a "Danish model" had emerged, which it described as a "Russian trace" allegedly being discovered and "exploited for a propaganda spectacle". It accused Denmark of "provocations" intending to "frighten the Danish population in order to justify... a prolonged confrontation with Russia".

Russian state media cite the foreign ministry in Moscow as saying it will respond to the expulsion of its official "accordingly".

In a statement on Saturday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said: "I strongly condemn the assassination attempt against a US-Ukrainian citizen in Denmark, orchestrated by Russian intelligence services.

"This was an attack on EU soil. And it is unacceptable," she said, adding that "Russia's hybrid threats are becoming less and less hybrid, and more and more real."

The rapper's real name is Albert Vasiliev.

Both individuals pleaded not guilty to the charges, local media reported.

In July, Russia's FSB security service accused Vasiliev and the Ukrainian authorities of organising a "terrorist attack" on military facilities and personnel in Russia. The rapper denied this allegation on social media.

In a statement on Friday, Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen said the alleged assassination attempt was Russian "intimidation" and an attempt to make Denmark "waver" in its support for Ukraine.

Russia's defence attaché must leave the country within seven days, Rasmussen said.

He also said Denmark wants the EU to restrict the ability of Russians to travel throughout Europe, saying even though Copenhagen was already very reluctant to issue visas, Russians could still get a Schengen visa in another country and travel to Denmark.

Copenhagen wants these visas to apply only in the country that has issued them, he added.
</article>

Title: Zelensky says Crimean Bridge strikes 'fair response' as he meets UK's Streeting
URL: https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6wy0qj7w5zqo

<article>
- Published

**Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has justified Kyiv's repeated attacks on a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, calling it a "fair response" to 109 separate Russian attacks on bridges in Ukraine.**

In comments to the BBC in Kyiv, Zelensky said the intense attacks on Ukraine by Russia that have followed the strikes on the Crimean Bridge were only a "signal that Vladimir Putin does not want to stop. He wants a reason to escalate".

He rejected the claim by the Russian president that the bridge - which links Russia to the peninsula it illegally annexed from Ukraine - was "exclusively civilian" in use.

"There are facts, not just the words of Putin. We can see," he said.

The Ukrainian president pointed to images online of tanks and other Russian military hardware using the route from Russia into occupied Crimea as a supply line and for logistics.

"If Putin used the internet, he could see that."

The Ukrainian president added that Russia had carried out attacks with missiles and drones on bridges in Ukraine.

This week's combined missile-and-drone strikes by Ukrainian forces destroyed the central road section of the Crimean Bridge, collapsing part of it together with one of the two support arches into the sea and rendering the structure unusable for road traffic.

Russian attacks on Ukraine continued on Friday evening and overnight: a seven-year-old boy was killed in missile and drone strikes on Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih in the central Dnipropetrovsk region. Local officials say he had been in a playground at the time.

A 20-year-old female medic was also killed. A local official added that when rescuers rushed to the scene, the same site was targeted again with jet powered drones. Another 58 people were injured in the city.

Ukraine's state emergency service DSNS said 11 people were also injured in the north-eastern Kharkiv region, and one person in Rivne, in the north-west.

Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Zelensky was speaking ahead of a meeting in Kyiv with UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who told the Ukrainian president he was here to show that Europe was united in its support.

"The more Putin tries to divide us, the more resolute we become," Streeting said.

He said that Russian missiles hitting Poland on Friday, during military exercises of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, was an "outrageous provocation".

The timing, Streeting said, seemed "more than a coincidence".

Asked by the BBC about Nato's response, he said the best way was to "do more for Ukraine" to defend itself against Putin who he called a "cold-blooded killer".

Streeting's description of Putin chimed with the comments made earlier by Zelensky, who described the Kremlin leader a "killer". This was done in response to US President Donald Trump referring this week to Putin as his "friend".

Streeting's visit to Kyiv came after European leaders meeting in Berlin on Thursday alongside US envoys said they were ready for negotiations with Moscow on ending the war in Ukraine.

"Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic".

Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, one of the two US envoys who were in Berlin, said the US president - who had also dialled into the meeting from Air Force One - wanted to make a deal with Moscow "with Europe by his side".

Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US-led peace talks - but earlier this week he invited European representatives to Moscow as it wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks".

That meeting in the German capital came hours after Putin had held historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen, China, with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Zelensky said he had been "sceptical" ahead of the latest round of talks, when US envoys claimed that Russia was prepared to make compromises to end the war.

"I thought \[Putin\] would find reason to escalate."

Speaking to the BBC, Streeting added: "Putin has absolutely no business playing the victim. He is the aggressor in this war. He provoked an illegal invasion of Ukraine. And all of us, right throughout the world, need to judge Putin not on his words, but on his actions."

In a separate development on Saturday, Finland said it "detected a drone strike on a Russian merchant vessel" in the eastern Gulf of Finland, "in an international maritime area".

The Finnish defence ministry said in a statement that the vessel was damaged, without giving any further details.

It added that "temporary restrictions on aviation and maritime areas in the eastern Gulf of Finland" were now reinstated for safety reasons.

Russia has not publicly commented on the issue.
</article>

Title: Russia-bound ship towed away after it was attacked in Gulf of Finland
URL: https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj752ddve27ko

<article>
- Published

**A Russian cargo vessel that was hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland is being towed away, authorities have said.**

The Sparta II had been bound for Russia's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad when it was hit on Saturday morning, sparking a fire aboard.

It then drifted into Finnish waters and its crew were evacuated to Russia. Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Kyiv has yet to comment.

Finland's Border Guard said on Sunday afternoon that fire was no longer visible from the outside but thermal cameras showed that some containers on the ship were still warm.

Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said two drones appeared to have been used in the strike and that there was "no threat" to his territory's supplies.

The Sparta II was sanctioned by the US in 2022 and Ukraine earlier this year, and is run by a Russian company, according to the Ukrainian and US governments.

The company says it was established within the structure of Russia's defence ministry in 2011 and since 2015 has been operating within the military construction complex.

Finland's coast guard said it had been alerted to the attack at around 08:50 local time (06:50 GMT) on Saturday and that the cargo vessel had been located approximately 50km west of the island of Suursaari in the Gulf of Finland.

This prompted "temporary aviation and maritime restrictions" around the area, Finnish border officials said.

"War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity," Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said. "Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor."

Shortly after the incident, Finland's defence ministry said a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating the country's airspace, potentially linked to "rescue or tracking operations".

While Besprozvannykh initially said the crew of the Sparta II intended to repair the ship and carry on their journey, the Finnish Border Guard later said they had been evacuated to another Russian vessel that was en route to Russia.

Jukka-Pekka Lumilahti, director of maritime operations at the Finnish Border Guard, said during a news conference on Sunday that one Sparta II crew member had suffered minor injuries.

The Russian rescue vessel Murman is leading towing operations with the support of a Finnish guard ship and a Estonian naval patrol vessel.

Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave that sits between Poland and Lithuania.

Finnish Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen said that the Border Guard was responsible for the investigation into the attack and was co-operating with other relevant authorities.

Nato has also been informed, the defence ministry said.

The Baltic Sea has become a flashpoint in the Russia-Ukraine war, triggered when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Ukraine has recently ramped up its long-range attacks against Russia beyond the front lines.

Earlier this month, a Ukrainian drone strike hit a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland.
</article>

Title: Boy, 7, pulled alive from rubble hours after Russian strike on Ukraine, rescuers say

**A seven-year-old boy has been rescued from the rubble of a residential building in Dymer, in the Kyiv region, after 14 hours. Overnight Russian strikes on the village killed 11 people, Ukrainian officials have said.**

The attack occurred in the early hours of Sunday. A 79-year-old woman was also rescued alive from the collapsed building, Kyiv's regional head Tymur Tkachenko said.

A strike on a private home in Bila Tserkva killed one more person and set the building ablaze, he added.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky also said three people were killed and 13 wounded in a separate strike on Vyshneve, also in the Kyiv region, that hit a grocery store on Sunday.

Ukrainian authorities said the boy in Dymer is in stable condition and was taken to hospital, and have thanked everyone involved in saving his life.

Zelensky and Ukraine's national police also confirmed the rescue of the boy.

In a Telegram post, Tkachenko said the 79-year-old woman rescued from the rubble was receiving treatment in hospital.

Earlier he said six people were injured in the attack, while others were still missing.

Zelensky said more than 130 people are involved in emergency operations at the scene, and that they will continue until they have "complete information about every single person".

Sending his condolences to the families and loved ones of those killed, he said the strike struck the residential building, "practically blowing a section of it to smithereens".

Zelensky added that "rescue efforts are complicated by constant new air raid alerts and renewed threats".

The strike hit the building at 05:00 local time, when families were still asleep, Ukraine's minister of internal affairs Ivan Vyhivskyi said.

More than 70 strikes have been launched across 10 Ukrainian regions as of Sunday evening, Vyhivskyi added.

In his video address posted online, Zelensky also said three people were killed and 13 injured in a strike on an "ordinary grocery store" in Vyshneve.

Mayor Illya Dikov wrote on social media that three children were among the injured.

Russia also struck a power substation in the Dnipropetrovsk region, Ukraine's Prime Minister Sergiy Koretsky said in a post on X., external

Title: 'They were all asleep': Ukrainians describe deadly overnight Russian apartment strike
URL: https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3j4r2elrvj8o

<article>
- Published

**All that was left of Tetiana's flat after the Russian strike was one outer wall with a satellite dish still clinging to it.**

A drone hit her apartment block in Dymer, near Kyiv, before dawn on Sunday, killing 11 of her neighbours.

Tetiana wasn't home. She spent the night in a nearby village, celebrating her 60th birthday.

Two residents of the building are still officially missing, though most of the wreckage has now been cleared.

The Russian attack happened as Ukrainian naval drones sank a Russian warship, the Merkury, which had docked for refuelling in Libya. The Angara cargo ship, which Kyiv says is used for military logistics and is on US and Ukrainian sanctions lists, was also hit.

"We are responding to Russia's aggression," President Volodymyr Zelensky said, calling both vessels legitimate targets.

He said the block of flats in Dymer, a village in the Kyiv region, had been struck by a Russian Shahed drone, possibly one of the jet-powered drones that travel at extremely high speeds and have been launched at Ukraine in large numbers in recent days.

Zelensky stressed that such weapons used foreign components, and he called for sanctions to be tightened.

"Every country and every leader who helps maintain pressure on the aggressor helps protect human life," he said.

But even hours after the initial attack, the danger had not passed.

Russia increasingly uses its drones to hit Ukraine just as rescuers go to work. They're known as "double-tap" attacks, and often deadly.

It makes the work of searching for survivors, which now happens every single day, extremely perilous.

In Dymer, all rescue work had to stop multiple times on Sunday as more Russian drones were detected overhead.

The emergency services, as well as residents and the press, had only moments to clear the scene and rush for shelter as Ukrainian fighter jets began shooting drones out of the sky.

Many people huddled in an underground kindergarten, decked out with children's paintings and balloons, the safest place around.

The number of civilians casualties here has been surging in recent weeks.

On Sunday, in the Kyiv region alone, four people were killed in two other deadly attacks - one on a supermarket. A young teacher was among the dead.

"This is the tactic of Russian Federation," Tymur Tkachenko, head of the regional military administration told us at the scene. "They are trying to make us scared. To stop Ukraine fighting. But they cannot do this with us."

But the aerial attacks - and retaliation - are now almost non-stop and their scope is widening.
</article>

Title: Russian warship hit by Ukrainian drones in Libya, Zelensky says
URL: https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr894gjz0j0yo

<article>
**A Russian warship was sunk by Ukrainian drones at a port in Libya on Sunday, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said.**

There was an explosion on the warship at the Benghazi naval base in the early morning, while it was docking for fuel and supplies ahead of its return to Russia, local authorities said.

Zelensky added that Ukraine's attack hit a second Russian vessel, a cargo ship which he claimed was being used to transport weapons.

The local health ministry said it had received injured people from a commercial ship that was targeted off the coast of the port. It is not clear whether this is the same vessel as the one Ukraine has claimed responsibility for.

Following the strikes, the Kremlin warned of an "escalation of tensions in the region", but declined to comment directly on the attacks in Libya.

Libya's two governments - the UN-recognised government in the capital, Tripoli, and a rival administration in the east - have both condemned the attack.

The eastern government, based in Benghazi, called it a violation of maritime safety and an attack on their sovereignty.

Seven naval drones were deployed to target and sink the corvette Merkury, one of Russia's newest ships, Zelensky said in a statement on Monday. He added that a Ka-27 combat helicopter was also destroyed.

The Ukrainian president said the second ship was the MV ANGARA, a Russian container carrier.

The attack came the day after a Russian cargo vessel was hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland. The Sparta II had been bound for Russia's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad when it was hit on Saturday morning.

Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely to be behind the attack. Kyiv has not commented.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Monday that the "expansion of terrorist activity in the Baltic" was a "dangerous trend" and has said "it is, of course, leading to an escalation of tensions in the region."

When questioned over the attacks in Libya, Peskov said information would be provided by the country's defence ministry and added: "We paid attention to Zelensky's statements about it".

Peskov declined to comment on the strikes on Russian ships in Libya and said that that information would be provided by Russia's Defence Ministry.

The UN mission in Libya expressed "serious concern" over the attacks on Sunday, calling for "an immediate, independent and transparent investigation".

Videos posted on social media and geolocated by BBC Verify show the ship that was struck in the morning engulfed in flames and smoke. Satellite imagery from Planet Labs PBC also shows a boat on fire at 05:47 GMT at the Benghazi port.

US-based intelligence firm Vantor collected high-resolution images that it said showed Project 20380 Steregushchiy-class corvette (Merkury) - a Russian navy ship - moored in the port on Saturday, and on Sunday showed most of the same ship capsized and sunk with only the forward bow still visible.

Neither of Libya's rival administrations has formally declared support for either side in the Russia-Ukraine war, but they have contrasting ties with Moscow and Kyiv.

The head of the Libyan National Army, which controls much of the east of the country, has longstanding links with Russia.

The eastern-based Government of National Stability (GNS) said the Russian ship - which it did not name or identify - was using the Benghazi port within the framework of an existing maritime agreement.

Sunday's incident is under investigation, and authorities are coordinating with their Russian counterparts to determine the source of the suspected attack and who is responsible for it, GNS added.

It said Libya was not party to the Russia-Ukraine war, or any other conflict beyond its borders.

GNS has accused the Tripoli-based Government of National Unity (GNU) of hosting Ukrainian military personnel and allowing them to operate from Libyan territory against Russian targets.

Separately, the GNU warned against hosting foreign forces and allowing them to use facilities in a statement published by state media.

Libya fractured into violence and instability after its leader Muammar Gaddafi was overthrown in 2011, leading to the opposing governments.

Benghazi is almost 3,000 km (1,864 miles) away from the Russian capital Moscow.

In March, Russia accused Ukraine of targeting the Russian tanker Arctic Metagaz in the Mediterranean between Libya and Malta with "uncrewed sea drones" launched from the Libyan coast.

As well as having an economic impact on Russia, hampering the ability of their so-called shadow fleet of tankers to export oil and gas, attacks like this are seen as humiliating to the Kremlin, according to Dr Jalel Harchaoui of the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI).

But it is not only Moscow that will want to react to this latest incident. The ship was in the region as part of a deal with the government of eastern Libya - allied with Khalifa Haftar, commander of the Libyan National Army.

Harchaoui said Haftar will take the attack as a personal slight. "You're going to have a response by the Haftar family. They will ask questions about who is hosting the Ukrainians."

*Additional reporting by Benedict Garman and Shayan Sardarizadeh, BBC Verify and Basma El Atti*
</article>

He defended the Arab countries' right to choose how to tackle climate change according to their national circumstances.

Title: Russian governor detained in rare criminal case against regional leader
URL: https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmwy868v3nneo

<article>
- Published

**The governor of Russia's northern Murmansk region has been arrested on corruption charges in the first detention of a regional leader for five years.**

Andrei Chibis, 47, is suspected of embezzlement and misappropriation of more than a billion roubles ($12.2.m; £9.3m) set aside to build an Arctic highway, as well as a further 39m roubles from the Murmansk construction budget.

Chibis is reported to have been detained as he arrived on a visit to Moscow on Monday and was taken in for questioning.

He denies wrongdoing but has made no public comment. His wife Yevgenia Chibis said "anyone who knows our family understands how ridiculous this is".

Chibis worked for several years as deputy minister for construction and housing, before becoming governor of Murmansk in 2019.

Murmansk is a key military point for Russia in the Arctic and is home to the Russian navy's Northern fleet.

Chibis was re-elected two years ago after surviving a knife attack and is considered an active supporter of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Governors are seen as representing the Kremlin, and Vladimir Putin removed several in the months after the war began in February 2022.

However, until now no regional governor has been arrested since the start of the war, even though plenty of high-ranking officials have been detained in that time.

The Murmansk governor is one of a number of officials suspected of corruption by the Russian interior ministry's investigative department which, according to reports, alleged that a criminal group was set up in 2022 to embezzle money from the regional budget and move it abroad, including to Kyrgyzstan.

Another part of the case involves alleged fraud surrounding the rebuilding of a motorway between the two Arctic towns of Apatity and Kirovsk, which are 15km (9.3 miles) apart.

According to Russian news agency Interfax, a court will decide whether Chibis will remain in custody at a hearing on Wednesday.

He has been sanctioned by both the UK and EU, which accuses him of involvement in the illegal transportation of Ukrainian children to Russia and their adoption by Russian families.
</article>

Title: South African court convicts Zimbabwean of trying to fight in Russia-Ukraine war
URL: https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmqj5qlj5yz9o

<article>
- Published

**A Zimbabwean national has been convicted by a court in South Africa of planning to go to fight in Ukraine.**

The country has strict laws which restrict unauthorised involvement in overseas wars.

South Africa's Foreign Military Assistance Act was passed in 1998 at a time when the government was concerned about members of the former apartheid security services going to fight elsewhere in Africa.

There has been growing concern across Africa over the recruitment of its citizens to fight in the war in Ukraine, with some reportedly being lured to Russia by promises of lucrative civilian employment.

A Ukrainian intelligence assessment estimated earlier this year that more than 1,700 people from 36 countries in Africa have been recruited to fight for Russia.

Some have been captured and are being held as prisoners of war.

In March, Kenya estimated that 252 of its citizens had been illegally conscripted in Russia.

Kenyan Foreign Minister Musalia Mudavadi visited Moscow to address the issue. He said an agreement had been reached for Russia to stop recruiting Kenyan nationals.

In the same month, Zimbabwe said that 15 of its nationals had been killed after being recruited to fight for Russia in Ukraine, with more than 60 still trapped on the frontlines.

The previous month, South Africa secured the return of 17 of its nationals who were allegedly tricked into joining the war.

South Africa's government said it condemned "the exploitation of young vulnerable people by individuals working with foreign military entities".

Ukraine has also been recruiting foreign nationals, including from Africa.

*Additional reporting by Khanyisile Ngcobo in Johannesburg.*
</article>

Title: Businesses supporting Ukraine told to 'act now' to protect against Russian sabotage
URL: https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckpdw4d0z2dwo

<article>
- Published

**The UK government has warned that any businesses providing support for Ukraine's armed forces could become a target for Russia, and should "act now" to protect themselves.**

An alert issued on Tuesday warned of an increased risk of Russian sabotage attacks such as arson and threats to staff, premises and operations.

Any businesses that are providing support to Ukraine's armed forces, including organisations in the supply chain, have been urged to take extra precautions, both physically and online.

Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and there has been a recent increase in Russian sabotage attempts against defence related facilities in Europe.

In September, a man appeared in court accused of planning to "torch" UK drone factories on behalf of Russia's intelligence services in an alleged sabotage plot.

Estonia has also accused Moscow of being behind an attempted arson attack at a drone factory last week, and Germany blamed it for a drone attack at Leipzig's airport in August.

The joint alert, external between MI5's National Protective Security Agency (NPSA) and the Ministry of Defence, has advised businesses to remove unnecessary detail that can be found online, emphasising that hostile reconnaissance usually begins with internet research.

"These actions so far are significant but not strategic. They cause disruption, dismay and some damage but they have not reached the level of them being a strategic threat to the security of Europe," Gen Barrons added.

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has warned that threats from Russia are aimed at deterring the UK's support for Ukraine, which "must not" happen.

Speaking to the Commons Foreign Affairs Committee earlier on Tuesday, Miliband said the threat from Moscow will endure beyond the Ukraine war and reiterated that any peace settlement must not reward Russia.

Security Minister Dan Jarvis said recent sabotage attempts across Europe "demonstrate the seriousness of the threats we face".

Minister for the Armed Forces, Louise Sandher-Jones, added that Russia and other hostile actors "pose a growing threat", while companies have a responsibility to strengthen their security "and help protect Britain".
</article>

Title: My family were killed in Ukraine. My mum blamed Zelensky's troops - the truth is complicated
URL: https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw24e17v9e51o

**I am sitting on my balcony in Kyiv looking at a photo of a garden in the village I grew up in, in eastern Ukraine. The plot is overgrown with thick grass, and two wooden stakes are planted in the ground. Despite the warm sunshine, I find myself shivering.**

The woman who sent me the photo says the stakes mark the graves of my grandparents, killed as the Ukrainian-Russian front line reached our little community. Not far away, in another garden in the village, the body of my father, Serezha, is buried in a greenhouse.

I cover the Russia-Ukraine war for the BBC World Service, but found myself in the middle of that story in February last year when my mother sent me a devastating text message.

"Granny, grandad and Serezha are gone. Now there is no-one left," it said.

It turned my world upside down.

Because not only had I lost three beloved family members, my mother blamed Ukraine for their deaths - the country where I was born and have lived for most of my life.

We stopped speaking.

Mum was born in Siberia. From the moment Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, she had supported Russia in the conflict.

Backing Moscow is not that unusual in the Donbas region - the predominantly Russian-speaking part of eastern Ukraine where my village Dachne is located.

After pro-Russian forces captured large parts of the Donbas in 2014, many of those who stayed supported Moscow over Kyiv, a stance cemented by exposure to Russian state TV.

Now the Russians occupy almost 80% of Donetsk - the part of the Donbas where my village is. Over the past nearly five years, since Russia's full-scale invasion, entire towns and cities have been razed to the ground, external.

I had already fallen out with my sister Sasha, who had been living in Moscow with her young family when the war broke out. She refused to take sides - I felt hurt and cut her off.

But earlier this year, around the first anniversary of dad's death, Sasha unexpectedly texted me. We started talking over text about our childhood - the way things used to be. I realised I was not angry with her anymore. She too was grieving, missing dad just as much as I was.

I started looking for witnesses to the events in Dachne that took place in January 2025, the month dad is believed to have been killed. It was not easy. It was a village of a few hundred people, but many had left, others had died, and those who remained had limited phone signals.

Russia publicly announced the capture of Dachne on 14 February and it has remained under Moscow's control ever since.

This meant it was impossible for me to travel there in person. So I began trying to contact my family's neighbours.

In a Dachne village messaging chat, I found the number of a man I'll call Misha. I was told he had been with my father on the day he died. Speaking to the BBC could put him in danger with the Russian occupiers, so I did not tell him I worked for the BBC or that I was recording our call.

Misha told me that on 26 January he had looked in on my father and realised he had been injured. Serezha told him he had been "clipped" by a drone, and had asked Misha to bring a first aid kit, he said.

It is impossible to know which side was operating the drone that killed my father, but we do know that Russian drones were constantly targeting the village at that time.

"I asked if the wound was serious. He \[Serezha\] said it wasn't," said Misha - but then recalling how, when he had returned to check on my father a couple of hours later, he had found him dead.

She could not recall what this date was, but knew it was in the second half of January.

At this time, she said, "the Russians were fully advancing - the edges of the village were being shelled. Then the Ukrainian soldiers moved from the edge of the village into the centre. They hid in people's yards and used side streets to avoid drones."

She said two soldiers entered her property. They had not been wearing any identifying insignia but had been speaking Ukrainian, she said - a language that Lina described as "Bandera", a derogatory term for Ukrainians.

"You're going to have to leave. Why are you still here?" Lina said they had asked her.

She had found the door to the house they had been staying in open, she said, despite the freezing conditions.

With drones buzzing overhead, Lina said she had not dared look inside, but had later heard from neighbours that my grandparents had been found dead. She believed it had been the Ukrainian soldiers who visited her house who had shot them.

Another neighbour, who I will call Maria, described discovering their bodies - my grandmother in bed, covered in a blanket, and my grandfather lying on the floor in a pool of now-dried blood.

Maria also believed Ukrainian soldiers had killed them - because, she said, that she too had felt threatened by Ukrainian troops at the time.

"If they had seen me they would have killed me too."

"Your grandparents caught them in a bad mood because your grandfather was always asking to be evacuated. And \[the soldiers\] were, you know, high. They were taking drugs. So your grandparents got in their way," she told me.

Most of the other people in the village I spoke to also believe Ukrainian soldiers killed them, though their testimony is not based on direct evidence.

The new local mayor, appointed by the Russian occupiers when they finally took control of Dachne in February, said she had been present at my grandparents' burial the following month, and said half of my grandmother's skull was missing.

These accounts of how they might have died in January 2025 were deeply disturbing, though no-one had witnessed their deaths and the information I was given could not be independently verified.

The villagers I spoke to - now living in occupied territory - did say there had been some tensions between themselves and Ukrainian troops at the time, because the soldiers had viewed those who remained in Dachne as supporters of Russia.

The clinical causes of my grandparents' deaths are unclear.

"I wasn't there. But why would you kill old people?" he asked.

I examined military maps from DeepStateMap.Live, an open-source Ukrainian resource, and US think tank Institute for the Study of War. They suggested Ukrainian forces still held the street where my grandparents lived during the week they had died, although the front line had been shifting rapidly.

My colleagues helped me identify the Russian military units that went on to capture Dachne. We found telephone numbers of Russian soldiers. But none of them agreed to speak to me.

I turned to the Ukrainian military.

A soldier from the 33rd Mechanised Brigade, who gave his name simply as Vlad, said his unit had still been in Dachne at the time my grandparents were believed to have died and that the Russians had been swiftly advancing.

Another Ukrainian soldier I spoke to also confirmed Ukraine's troops had still been in control of some parts of Dachne in late January.

We put our findings on the deaths of my grandparents to the Ukrainian military.

The Donetsk regional prosecutor's office, which is now based outside Russian-controlled territory, has documented alleged Russian war crimes reported by eyewitnesses in villages around Dachne during December 2024 and January 2025 - including the killing of five civilians in a basement in the nearby village of Kostyantynopilske.

However, Ukrainian investigators have no equivalent cases registered in Dachne during that period. They have documented only three deaths there. My father and grandparents are not among them.

Their bodies lie in occupied territory, and I do not know if I will ever be able to say goodbye properly and bury them with dignity.

Title: Russia's own figures show it has lost nearly 500,000 people in Ukraine war
URL: https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmx27g533zwyo

<article>
**At least 490,334 Russian soldiers have died since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022, according to Russian government statistics analysed by the BBC.**

The leaked Rosstat data reveal how the full-scale invasion of Ukraine has fundamentally changed mortality patterns in Russia, and show the high cost paid in human life in a war that Vladimir Putin had assumed would last only days but is now almost five years old.

BBC Russian has had access to more than 11 million death records from 2021 to September 2026, after a hack by Belarusian group Cyber Partisans BY and Ukraine's Silent Crow.

Russia's statistics agency admitted to a cyber-attack, but denied any protected information had been leaked.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Wednesday that only Russia's defence ministry could officially report data on losses: "I suggest no other data be taken into account." The defence ministry has not released any official casualty figures for several years.

Together with independent Russian outlet Mediazona, BBC Russian has compared the Rosstat data with its own list of confirmed military deaths, pulled from open sources since the start of the invasion, and it has found matches for 90% of the records.

Military experts estimate that the BBC's list of 290,012 deaths, gleaned from official reports, social media, new memorials and graves, may account for 45-55% of the true death toll, which would range from 527,295 to 644,471.

The records show that 65% of 18 to 24 year-olds in Russia who lost their lives in 2025 died in the war. For those aged 25-34 the number was 59%. Only among 45 to 54 year-olds does cardiovascular disease claim more Russian lives than the conflict.

The data also reveal the extent of losses in specific areas of Ukraine. Some 20,000 Russian soldiers died fighting for control of 10 Ukrainian villages whose combined pre-war population was 12,000.

During the fight for one small village called Andriivka, south of the town of Bakhmut in Donetsk region, 1,122 Russians lost their lives. Before the war 74 people lived there.

Russia does not give public figures for losses sustained since the war began in February 2022. And two years ago Rosstat stopped publishing data of deaths from external causes, which was used to gauge the extent of military losses.

For example, only 70% of deaths we have established of soldiers from the occupied regions of Donetsk and Luhansk in eastern Ukraine who fought in the Russian army were accounted for in the Rosstat files.

Overall, the Rosstat dataset confirms the trends that we have observed with our own count.

Ukrainian losses were last put at about 50,000 by President Volodymyr Zelensky in July 2026, but another list based on open sources by the anonymous UA Losses website puts the figure at 115,952.

## How we came to a figure near half a million

The Rosstat dataset contains no names but does include ages, places of residence, places of death and also circumstances of death.

We have filtered the records first by location, leaving only Ukraine as well as Russian border regions that saw incursions by the Ukrainian army.

Next, we identified 425,174 entries explicitly indicating a military-related cause of death, such as explosions or shrapnel during combat operations.

As this count could include civilians, we filtered out women as well as men outside the 18-65 age group. And if someone lived and died in the four Ukrainian regions occupied by Russia, we excluded them as a possible civilian – unless he had a record of military service attached to his entry.

Another 14,093 entries were identified by looking at employment, and 51,067 were recorded in the database as deceased on the basis of a court ruling. This often happens when a soldier goes missing in a combat zone for more than six months and their body has not been recovered.

Again, we filtered out civilians by only counting deaths in the war zones in Ukraine and Russia.

According to BBC Russian's analysis of the leaked files, in the first year of the war the average age of those killed was 34. By 2025, as prisoners and contract soldiers entered the ranks, it had risen to 40 (38 according to our own list).

Some of Russia's poorest regions in Eastern Siberia account for a disproportionately large share of the losses. Men from Tyva, Buryatia and Zabaykalsky Krai are 20-25 times more likely to die in the war than residents of the biggest cities of Moscow and St Petersburg.

In most regions, the distribution of deaths based on Rosstat data differs from that in the BBC's list by just a few tenths of a percentage point.

At least 5,017 foreigners are among those who died fighting for Russia, according to our analysis of the Rosstat files, including 1,031 Uzbeks and 720 Tajiks. We have left out Ukrainians from this count to avoid including civilians.

This is a conservative estimate as dual nationals are listed as Russians in the database, and there is no reference to North Koreans who died repelling the Ukrainian incursion into Russia in 2024.

The BBC identified 2,304 North Korean soldiers who died there by analysing satellite imagery and official photographs of a newly built memorial in Pyongyang.

The leaked Russian statistics may not be complete but taken in conjunction with BBC Russian's own work they are significant.

In the context of a war that has lasted four years and 10 months, these are high numbers for Russia, when compared with the Soviet war in Afghanistan that ended in 1989.

In that 10-year war, an estimated 15,000 Red Army troops died, and an estimated one million civilians were killed.
</article>

Title: Five Russian military jets hit in airfield strike, says Ukraine
URL: https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck9q8xp5r5pgo

<article>
- Published

**Ukraine has said it damaged five Russian military aircraft in an attack on Russia's Savasleyka airfield, 300km (185 miles) east of Moscow.**

Three MiG-31 and two Su-34s aircraft were hit, Kyiv's General Staff said, adding that the extent of the damage was still being assessed but that "there may be even better news to come". It did not elaborate on what weapons it had used to hit the airfield.

Russia has not commented on the strikes.

The airfield at Savasleyka, in Russia's Nizhny Novgorod region, has been a target for Ukraine for several years. It hosts aircraft used by Russia to launch hypersonic missiles and glide bombs.

The take-off of MiG-31s in particular frequently triggers nationwide alerts across Ukraine, as the Kinzhal missiles they carry have been known to hit large infrastructure and military targets and are difficult to shoot down.

Overnight, Kyiv also said it hit two oil refineries in Russia's Samara region some 800km (500 miles) from the front line – the latest in a series of long-range strikes which have dented Moscow's oil processing capacity.

"Did you repair them? We'll hit them again," the defence ministry in Kyiv said.

Samara region governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said the night-time attacks had been "a true ordeal", with more than 145 drones shot down. One person was killed and several towns experienced power outages, Fedorishchev said.

Kyiv also said it had hit a radar system as well as fuel and logistics depots across Ukrainian territories currently occupied by Russia.

"Without fuel, military vehicles cannot move; without ammunition, artillery falls silent," the defence ministry said, adding that every successful hit meant Moscow could carry out fewer strikes.

Kyiv has developed a thriving weapons industry and Ukrainian strikes on Russian targets well beyond the front line have become commonplace in the years since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion.

On Tuesday, President Vladimir Putin called for a tightening of security measures across the country's energy facilities.

But he also argued that Russia had managed to stabilise its domestic fuel market without suffering "critical damage" and added that Moscow would "inevitably" retaliate against Kyiv.

Ukraine continues to come under daily attack. Ten people were killed across several regions between 24 and 25 November, while thousands are without power after Russian strikes on energy infrastructure.
</article>

Title: North Korea expels Swiss diplomat in sanctions row
URL: https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cq0l34e4kkr5o

<article>
North Korea has ordered Switzerland's diplomatic representative to leave the country within 48 hours and called for the office to close, in a row over sanctions.

It followed Switzerland's decision to place sanctions on the Songdowon international children's camp in the eastern city of Wonsan, which is attended by Russian and Chinese children among other nationalities.

The camp has been accused of involvement in transferring children from Russian-occupied areas of Ukraine.

North Korea's state-run news agency KCNA called the sanctions "a blatant hostile act".

Switzerland's department of foreign affairs said the country "distinguishes between its sanctions policy and its commitment to maintaining dialogue with all countries".

It added: "The reopening of the office in Pyongyang did not in any way affect Switzerland's implementation of UN sanctions related to North Korea's nuclear programme, nor its implementation of EU sanctions targeting North Korea in the context of Russia's war against Ukraine."

Thousands of North Korean soldiers have been deployed to help support Russia's war with Ukraine.

In August, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky accused Moscow of using North Korean missiles.
</article>
